title: Why Critical Mineral Shortages Are a CEO Issue
gist: BCG argues industrial CEOs understate critical-mineral exposure through three blind spots (spend-weighted views, tier-one-only mapping, ignoring processing and ownership), with demand 120-250% of supply through 2040. It says mapping exposure precisely also unlocks about $65 billion of largely unspent public capital, citing Siemens Gamesa, Mitsui and Traxys.

insights.claim: BCG's proprietary model has demand for key inputs including rare earths, graphite, copper and lithium running at roughly 120% to 250% of forecast supply through 2040.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Structural deficit across several metals supports a long-duration bullish view on supply-side assets and pricing power.
insights.locator: Three Blind Spots Understate the Risk

insights.claim: Batteries and electrification together are projected to increase critical-mineral demand 20-fold by 2040, while the AI buildout triples demand and defense spending quadruples it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: AI and defense are named as incremental demand legs beyond EVs, widening the set of buyers competing for scarce inputs.
insights.locator: Three Blind Spots Understate the Risk

themes.theme: Mosquito minerals: tiny spend, total stoppage

insights.claim: The most dangerous mineral exposures are often small-value inputs that never reach the risk register yet halt entire high-value production chains, so dollar-weighted procurement analysis systematically misprices risk.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Companies with trivial-spend, no-substitute inputs carry hidden downside; screen for these rather than copper/lithium headline names.

insights.claim: Rare earths are roughly 40% of a magnet's cost but under 1% of the value of the electric vehicle that needs the magnet, and a fighter jet's ~20 kg of rare earths is worth less than its paint.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows the extreme asymmetry between input cost and disruption impact that gives rare-earth holders leverage over OEMs.

insights.claim: Gallium is a market under $350 million a year with ~900 tons of production, yet about $3.5 trillion of final products (logic and power chips, AI GPUs, 5G and satellite components) depend on it, often without ready substitutes.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A roughly 10,000x ratio of dependent product value to market size makes gallium a potential choke point for AI hardware supply.

insights.claim: Germanium prices roughly quadrupled in western markets after Chinese export licensing in 2023, a ban on exports to the US in 2024 and a cut-off of Japan in early 2026, trading at a substantial premium to Chinese volumes.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shows how export controls create a two-tier price market; watch for the same playbook on gallium, arsenic and tungsten.

insights.claim: Ultra-high-purity arsenic (7N5, used in GaAs semiconductors for 5G/6G, AI data-center optics, radar and defense electronics) is a ~$50 million upstream market where China controls ~90% of refining and a single Japanese producer supplies ~60% of the world's supply.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A single-facility, seismically exposed chokepoint for advanced and defense electronics that almost no company lists as a risk.

insights.claim: Mosquito minerals are often byproducts of other mining and industrial processes, so their supply follows the host metal's economics and a price spike does not reliably call forth new production.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Price signals fail to fix shortages here, so spikes can persist longer than in primary commodities.

themes.theme: Hidden exposure in tier-two and process inputs

insights.claim: A company that buys almost no critical minerals directly can still be acutely exposed because minerals arrive embedded in motors, magnets, power modules, lasers and sensors.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Tier-one supplier data and bills of materials understate exposure; diligence should look at embedded content.

insights.claim: Minerals are also embedded in production processes (crucibles, sputtering targets, furnace internals, catalysts, dies, capital equipment), so a manufacturer can be halted by shortages of materials it never purchases.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Process inputs create dependencies invisible to any product-level mapping.

insights.claim: Precision machining of turbine blades, engine blocks and aerospace parts depends on tungsten carbide cobalt-bonded cutting tools, with tungsten concentrated in China (tightening export licensing) and cobalt in the DRC.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Aerospace and industrial output is exposed to tungsten and cobalt via consumable tooling.

insights.claim: Processing rather than mining is the bottleneck for many minerals: China refines roughly 90% of rare earths, 65-70% of lithium and cobalt and about 70% of graphite, and Australia ships over 90% of its spodumene to China.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Mine-country diversification does little if refining remains in China; processing capacity outside China is the scarce asset.

insights.claim: Maps of asset location and asset ownership can differ radically: the DRC produces about two-thirds of mined cobalt with major operations majority-owned by Chinese companies, and Chinese firms own a majority of Indonesia's nickel refining, which hosts nearly 70% of upstream nickel capacity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Switching a contract from a Chinese to an Indonesian refinery may not reduce geopolitical exposure.
insights.quote: Moving a supply contract from a Chinese refinery to an Indonesian one may not change a company’s geopolitical risk exposure.

themes.theme: Public capital as a competitive lever

insights.claim: Advanced-economy public finance commitments to critical minerals reached about $65 billion in 2025, over four times the 2023 level, but most is committed and unspent, with some countries having spent under 10% or nothing as of mid-2026.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A large pipeline of government money still to be deployed into mineral projects over coming quarters.
insights.locator: A Missed Opportunity to Access Public Funds

insights.claim: Public vehicles are meant as a catalyst, equal to about one-tenth of capital needed through 2040, and carry conditions such as reporting obligations, governance rights, localization requirements and screening.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Government funds cover only a small share of need, so private capital must fill the gap, with strings attached.

insights.claim: Offtake commitments are typically the primary eligibility gate for government-backed co-investment and guarantee vehicles, so companies that cannot quantify their exposure cannot make credible offtake commitments and miss the funding.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: End users that sign offtakes can pull public capital into projects; offtake signers are enablers of project financing.

insights.claim: Siemens Gamesa signed a binding five-year neodymium and praseodymium supply contract with Arafura Rare Earths (200 t/yr in 2026 rising to 400 t/yr by year three) structured to satisfy Germany's condition for a up to $600 million export-credit guarantee, and Germany's development bank later added direct investment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An end-user offtake unlocked state financing for its own supplier, a template for Western rare-earth project funding.

insights.claim: Mitsui obtained the right to 40% of Josemaria copper concentrate (about 77,000 t/yr, first production around 2030) via a JOGMEC public tender rather than a private deal with owners BHP and Lundin Mining.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: State agencies can hold and re-tender offtake rights, giving government-linked buyers privileged access to supply.

insights.claim: Project Vault, a roughly $12 billion US stockpile of about $2 billion private capital and a $10 billion Export-Import Bank loan, pays trading firms Traxys, Hartree Partners and Mercuria to source rare earths, cobalt, gallium and other minerals.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Commodity traders gain a new paid strategic-reserve role, and Vault procurement is a new source of offtake demand for junior miners.

insights.claim: Since Project Vault's announcement, Traxys has signed offtakes with Abenojar Tungsten, NioCorp Developments, Arafura Rare Earths and Andromeda Metals covering high-purity alumina, ferroniobium, scandium oxide and tungsten concentrate.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Named juniors are early beneficiaries of US stockpile-linked offtake demand.

themes.theme: Resilience portfolio and what not to do

insights.claim: Resilience requires a portfolio of five escalating moves: map exposure, diversify early, design out dependence, recover materials through circular design, and secure supply through access and control, and these can also create pricing power and preferred-supplier status.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Provides a checklist for assessing how seriously an industrial is managing mineral risk.

insights.claim: One company that mapped material flows end to end with BCG found $5 billion of value at risk across more than 15 commodities that appeared nowhere in its procurement data.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Scale of hidden exposure suggests many industrials' disclosed mineral risk is understated.

insights.claim: Diversification is the cheapest measure but the one most likely to be theater, because broadening a component supplier base achieves nothing if all suppliers trace to the same upstream chokepoint.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Discount management claims of supplier diversification unless they address processing and ownership concentration.
insights.quote: It is the least-expensive measure but also the one most likely to be theater.
insights.locator: How Not to Manage Critical Minerals Risk

insights.claim: Overinsuring is a real cost: excess stockpiles and unnecessary offtake agreements lock up capital against risks that may not materialize, and one lithium acquisition was abandoned after diligence, avoiding a likely write-down from the price cycle.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Vertical integration and stockpiling late in a price cycle can destroy value, and restraint can be the right call.
insights.locator: How Not to Manage Critical Minerals Risk

insights.claim: Design flexibility reduces single points of failure, as when Tesla switched to cobalt-free iron-phosphate batteries and as copper-or-aluminum windings let manufacturers switch on price or availability without requalifying products.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Product designs with multi-material tolerance are less exposed to mineral shocks.

insights.claim: Circularity can turn an installed base into a captive mine, and closed-loop models like leased precious-metal catalysts, where platinum-group metals are reclaimed and re-refined, keep metal ownership from transferring.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Companies with leasing or take-back models may enjoy structural supply advantages in constrained metals.

insights.claim: Control-oriented measures such as take-or-pay offtakes, strategic inventory and upstream equity or joint ventures should be a last resort because they add overexposure to market cycles.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Upstream integration by industrials adds cyclical risk to the buyer's balance sheet.

insights.claim: Lead time should be treated as a form of scarcity: a widely available mineral that takes three years to requalify behaves operationally like a scarce one, as titanium for aerospace shows.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Qualification cycle length, which most frameworks omit, determines which inputs are real chokepoints.
insights.quote: Treat lead time as a form of scarcity.

insights.claim: When a mineral is physically available but price-volatile, accessible measures like design flexibility suffice, but when it is cheap with no substitute, such as rare-earth magnets or high-purity arsenic, a shortage stops production and circularity or control are needed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Distinguishing cost risk from availability risk determines the right and the affordable hedge.
insights.locator: Is the concern cost or availability?
